What "clean" actually means on this page

Clean is three separate screens stacked together, not one soft label. A bar has to clear all three to make this list: an A or B ingredient quality grade, no artificial sweeteners, and no processed oils.

59.2% of the 1298 bars in our database fail at least one of these. Here's how often each screen catches a bar, and where it usually shows up.

Ingredient Quality Grade C or Below
562 bars43.3%
The most common reason a bar fails the clean screen. A C, D, or F grade usually means synthetic additives, excess added sugar, or ultra-processed protein blends outweighing the ingredient list's strengths.
Affects: at least one flavor from 101 of 198 brands we track
Artificial Sweeteners
241 bars18.6%
Usually shows up as a flavor-rounding sweetener in low-sugar or high-fiber bars, often alongside allulose or fiber syrups to hit a specific sugar number on the label.
Found in: 1st Phorm, Addra Labs, Anabar, Atkins

What actually makes a protein bar clean

Search for clean protein bars and most lists filter on a vibe: "real food," "no junk," a short ingredient list. We don't screen on a feeling. Clean here means three specific pass or fail checks: an A or B ingredient quality grade, zero artificial sweeteners, zero processed oils. A bar clears the screen only if it passes all three, not just the one that's easiest to market.

The two ingredient-side checks exist because they target different problems than a macro number can catch. Artificial sweeteners (sucralose, acesulfame potassium, aspartame, saccharin) show up in bars that already look great on paper, low sugar, high protein, because a synthetic sweetener is the cheapest way to hit those numbers without using more sugar. Processed oils (canola, soybean, palm, hydrogenated oils) do the same thing for texture and shelf life. Neither shows up on a nutrition panel the way sugar or fat grams do. You have to read the ingredient list to catch them, which is exactly what a macro-based guide like Low Sugar + High Protein doesn't check for.

The A or B grade requirement is what stops a bar from qualifying just by avoiding those two ingredients. Our ingredient scoring weighs protein source quality and position in the ingredient list too, so a bar that skips artificial sweeteners and seed oils but leans on a low-quality protein blend or a long list of minor additives still won't clear the bar.

Four questions worth asking before you call a bar clean:
  • What's the sweetener, a natural sugar or sugar alcohol, or one of the four synthetic ones we screen for?
  • What's the primary fat source, a refined seed oil, or something less processed like nut butter or coconut oil?
  • Where does the protein come from, a single quality source, or a stack of isolates and blends that drags the grade down?
  • Does the ingredient quality grade actually back that up, or is a clean-sounding brand still scoring C or below?

Clean and healthy aren't the same claim. A bar can clear every screen on this page and still run high in calories or sugar, since none of the three criteria here look at macros. If you want to combine a clean ingredient screen with your own sugar, calorie, or protein targets, the Bar Finder lets you stack both at once.

What we found screening 1298 bars for clean criteria

59.2%
of bars fail at least one clean criterion
768 of 1298 bars fail the ingredient grade, the artificial sweetener screen, the processed oil screen, or some combination of the three. 476 of those fail more than one screen at once.
Processed oils disqualify almost as many bars as low grades.
603 bars (46.5%) contain a processed oil, ahead of the 562 bars (43.3%) that score a C grade or below. Between the two, ingredient-list quality problems outnumber sweetener problems by a wide margin.
Most disqualified bars fail more than one screen.
476 of the 768 disqualified bars fail two or all three criteria at once. Only 133 fail on grade alone, 145 on processed oils alone, and just 14 on artificial sweeteners alone.
Barebells and Quest fail completely.
Every tracked flavor from both brands contains an artificial sweetener and a processed oil, and most also score C or below. Neither brand has a single flavor that clears the clean screen.
Whole-food brands dominate the qualifying pool.
Larabar, Perfect Bar, Healthy Eating on the Go, Kize, RXBAR, and Bearded Bros all qualify at or near 100%, mostly built around dates, nuts, and whole-food protein sources instead of processed blends.
A mixed lineup is common.
NuGo qualifies at 0% (0 of 30 flavors), KIND at just 6.5% (2 of 31). Even brands with a reputation for clean eating rarely clear the bar across their entire lineup.
Disqualified bars average more protein than qualifying ones.
Bars that fail the clean screen average 14.5g protein versus 11.4g for bars that pass, a reminder that higher protein numbers often come from processed protein blends and synthetic sweeteners doing the work.
117 of 198 brands still clear at least one flavor.
Even with 59.2% of the database disqualified, more than half of the brands we track have at least one bar that passes all three clean criteria.

Frequently asked questions

For this guide, clean means three things at once: an A or B ingredient quality grade, no artificial sweeteners (sucralose, acesulfame potassium, aspartame, saccharin), and no processed oils (canola, soybean, palm, or hydrogenated oils). 530 of 1298 bars in our database meet all three criteria.
Cleaner ingredients generally means fewer synthetic additives, more whole-food protein sources, and less dependence on ultra-processed fats and sweeteners. That said, macros still matter. A clean bar can still be high in calories or sugar even if the ingredient list is excellent.
476 of the 768 disqualified bars fail more than one criterion at once, usually a processed oil and a below-B grade together. Manufacturers reach for cheap refined oils and synthetic sweeteners to hit specific price, shelf-life, or macro targets, and those same shortcuts tend to drag the ingredient score down too.
No. Every tracked flavor from both brands contains an artificial sweetener and a processed oil, and most also score C or below on ingredient quality. Neither brand has a single flavor that clears this guide's screen.
530 bars across 117 brands clear our clean screen, led by whole-food brands like Larabar, Perfect Bar, and Healthy Eating on the Go that qualify at or near 100%. The full ranked list is in the table below, sorted by ingredient quality.
It depends on your standard. Erythritol is a naturally occurring sugar alcohol, but commercially it's derived through fermentation of glucose, often from corn. We score it as a neutral-to-minor concern rather than an automatic disqualifier, so bars with erythritol can still earn A or B grades and appear on this list if the rest of the ingredient list is strong.
Egg whites, whey protein concentrate, and whole-food sources like nuts and seeds score highest. Whey isolate and pea protein score slightly lower but are still solid. Collagen protein scores as a concern because it lacks the essential amino acids needed for muscle protein synthesis.
Yes, and it's common. NuGo qualifies at 0% (0 of 30 flavors), KIND at just 6.5% (2 of 31). Check the Mixed Lineups table below before assuming a brand's whole lineup is clean just because one flavor is.
We update the database when new bars are added or when brands change their formulas. The scoring methodology stays consistent so grades are comparable across updates. The current data reflects August 2026.
